english_sentences: It has been stated by us in the preceding parts that, as this [moisture] is poured out and then congealed by the faculty residing in the affected bone, the [410] callus grows over the lips of the broken bone.

And when this has come about sufficiently, the lips of the fracture are bound together and tightened, not through the affected bone being joined (?) throughout its depth, as fleshes are joined (?), but, as has been said, at the outer surface, like a kind of band put about (?) [it].
All that follows is clear to those who pay attention.
For the seat is hemmed in, and the bandages become bunched together in this narrow space.
And again, those passed round the girdle cannot be girt so firmly as not to force the girdle to ride upward, and in this way all the bandagings would necessarily slacken.

One would seem to come nearest, though even so not achieving much, if one passed some of the bandages round the girdle and with most of the bandages applied the original bandaging; for in this way the bandagings would be most stable and would support one another.

beads.greek: τὰ μὲν οὖν πλεῖστα εἴρηται ὅσα καταλαμβάνει [411] τοὺς τὴν κληῖδα καταγνυμένους, προσξυνιέναι δὲ καὶ τόδε χρὴ, ὅτι κληῒς ὡς ἐπὶ τὸ πουλὺ κατάγνυται, ὥστε τὸ μὲν ἀπὸ τοῦ στήθεος πεφυκὸς ὀστέον εἰς τὸ ἄνω μέρος ὑπερέχειν, τὸ δὲ ἀπὸ τῆς ἀκρωμίης πεφυκὸς ὀστέον ἐν τῷ κάτω μέρει εἶναι.
beads.english: Now, most of the things that befall [411] those who break the collarbone have been stated; but one must also understand this further point, that the collarbone for the most part breaks in such a way that the bone growing from the chest projects toward the upper part, while the bone growing from the acromion lies in the lower part.

beads.greek: αἴτια δὲ τούτων τάδε, ὅτι τὸ μὲν στῆθος οὔτε κατωτέρω ἂν πουλὺ οὔτε ἀνωτέρω χωρήσειεν.
beads.english: The causes of these things are these: that the chest could move neither much lower nor much higher.

beads.greek: Οὐκ ἔστι σύνθετον ὄνομα τὸ στενυγροχωρίῳ ἐκ τε τοῦ ὑγροῦ καὶ τοῦ στενοῦ καὶ τῆς χώρας γεγονὸς, ὥς τινες νομίζουσιν, ἀλλ’ ἀπὸ τοῦ στενυγρὸν, ὅπερ οὐδ’ αὐτὸ πλέον σημαίνει τοῦ στενοῦ κατὰ παραγωγήν τινα γεγενημένης στενυγροχωρίας μηδὲν πλέον δηλούσης τῆς στενότητος.
beads.english: The word stenygrochōriē ('in a narrow space') is not a compound formed from hygron ('moist'), stenon ('narrow') and chōra ('place'), as some suppose. Rather, stenygrochōria has come about by a kind of derivation from stenygron, which itself signifies nothing more than stenon ('narrow'), so that stenygrochōria indicates nothing more than narrowness.

beads.greek: εὔδηλον δὲ τοῦτο κἀξ ὧν Σιμωνίδης εἶπεν, ὧδέ πως ἐχόντων· οὔπω τις οὕτω δασκίοις ἐν οὔρεσιν ἀνὴρ λέγονται δὶς ἐν οὐδὲ πάρδαλιν μοῦνος στενυγρῷ συντυχὼν ἐν ἀτραπῷ. ψιλοῦται δὲ δηλονότι κατὰ τὴν δευτέραν συλλαβήν.
beads.english: This is quite clear also from what Simonides said, which runs roughly thus: 'never yet has any man thus in the shadowy mountains [λέγονται δὶς ἐν: corrupt] nor a leopard, alone, meeting it on a narrow (stenygros) path.' And the word evidently has the smooth breathing at the second syllable.

beads.greek: [412] Μικρὸς γὰρ ὁ κιγκλισμὸς τοῦ ἄρθρου τοῦ ἐν τῷ στήθει.
beads.english: [412] For the oscillation of the joint at the chest is small.

beads.greek: Τὴν βραχεῖαν κίνησιν ὠνόμασε κιγκλισμόν.
beads.english: He has called a slight movement *kinklismos* ('wagging').

beads.greek: εἰ δ’ ἀπὸ τοῦ ζώου τοῦ κίγκλου γέγονε τοὔνομα, διότι κινεῖ συνεχῶς ἐκεῖνο τὰ πηγάνεια πτέρνα ἢ ἀπό τινος ἄλλου τῆς προκειμένης πραγματείας, οὐκ ἔστιν οἰκεῖον, ἀλλὰ μᾶλλον δεῖται αἰτίαν εἰπεῖν, δι’ ἣν ἡ πρὸς τὸ στέρνον τῆς κλειδὸς διάρθρωσις οὐ τῶν μικροτάτων οὖσα, καθάπερ ἕτεραί τινες, ὅμως οὐκ ἔχει κίνησιν ἀξιόλογον.
beads.english: Whether the name derives from the animal *kinklos* (the wagtail), because that bird continually moves its rump(?) feathers, or from something else, is not germane to the present treatise. What is needed instead is to state the cause on account of which the articulation of the collarbone with the breastbone, although it is not among the smallest, as certain others are, nevertheless has no appreciable movement.

beads.greek: αὐτὸς οὖν ὁ Ἱπποκράτης ἥντινα λέγει τούτου τὴν αἰτίαν εἶναι διὰ τῆς λέξεως ἀκούσωμεν.
beads.english: Let us then hear from the text itself what Hippocrates himself says the cause of this is.

beads.greek: στῆθος δὲ ἔοικεν οὐ τὸ σύμπαν λέγειν χωρίον, ὅσον ἐν τοῖς πρόσω τοῦ θώρακός ἐστιν, ἀλλὰ τὸ μέσον ὀστοῦν, ἐν ᾧ διαρθροῦνται πλευραὶ, ὃ καλοῦσιν ἰδίως οἱ μετ’ αὐτὸν ἰατροὶ στέρνον, ὅπερ ἀληθῶς εἶπεν.
beads.english: By 'chest' (*stêthos*) he seems to mean not the whole region at the front of the thorax, but the middle bone in which the ribs articulate, which the physicians after him call specifically *sternon*; and this he said truly.

He has called a slight movement *kinklismos* ('wagging').
Whether the name derives from the animal *kinklos* (the wagtail), because that bird continually moves its rump(?) feathers, or from something else, is not germane to the present treatise.

What is needed instead is to state the cause on account of which the articulation of the collarbone with the breastbone, although it is not among the smallest, as certain others are, nevertheless has no appreciable movement.
Let us then hear from the text itself what Hippocrates himself says the cause of this is.

By 'chest' (*stêthos*) he seems to mean not the whole region at the front of the thorax, but the middle bone in which the ribs articulate, which the physicians after him call specifically *sternon*; and this he said truly.

beads.greek: [413] Αὐτὸ γὰρ ἑωυτῷ συνεχές ἐστι τὸ στῆθος καὶ τῇ ῥάχει.
beads.english: [413] For the chest is continuous both with itself and with the spine.

beads.greek: Τὸ μὲν οὖν ἑαυτῷ συνεχὲς εἶναι τὸ στέρνον ἐναργῶς φαίνεται· τὸ δὲ τῇ ῥάχει νοηθήσεται σαφῶς, ἐὰν σκελετῷ ζώῳ τὰς πλευράς ποτε ἴδῃς ἐναργῶς ἐρηρεισμένας ὀπίσω μὲν ἐπὶ τῆς ῥάχεως, ἔμπροσθεν δὲ πρὸς τὸ στέρνον.
beads.english: That the breastbone is continuous with itself is plainly evident; that it is continuous with the spine will be clearly understood if you ever see, in a skeleton of an animal, the ribs plainly resting behind upon the spine and in front against the breastbone.

beads.greek: Ἄγχιστα μὲν ἡ κληῒς πρὸς τὸ τοῦ ὤμου ἄρθρον πλοώδης ἐστίν· ἠνάγκασται γὰρ πυκινοκίνητος εἶναι διὰ τὴν τῆς ἀκρωμίης σύζευξιν.
beads.english: Nearest to the joint of the shoulder the collarbone is loose (?); for it is compelled to be frequently moved on account of its junction with the acromion.

beads.greek: ἄλλως τε ὅταν τρωθῇ, φεύγει ἐς τὸ ἄνω μέρος τὸ πρὸς τῷ στήθει προσεχόμενον καὶ οὐ μάλα ἐς τὸ κάτω μέρος ἀναγκάζεσθαι ἐθέλει.
beads.english: Besides, when it is injured, the part attached at the chest escapes upward, and is not very willing to be forced into the lower position.

beads.greek: καὶ γὰρ πέφυκε κοῦφον καὶ ἡ εὐρυχωρίη αὐτῷ ἄνω πλείων ἢ κάτω.
beads.english: For it is naturally light, and the open space for it is greater above than below.

beads.greek: ὁ δὲ ὦμος καὶ τὰ προσηρτημένα τούτοισιν εὐαπόλυτά εἰσιν ἀπὸ τῶν πλευρέων καὶ τοῦ στήθεος καὶ διὰ τοῦτο δύναται καὶ ἀνωτέρω πουλὺ ἀνάγεσθαι καὶ κατωτέρω.
beads.english: But the shoulder and the parts attached to these are easily detached from the ribs and the chest, and for this reason it can be drawn both much higher and lower.

greek_sentences: [413] Αὐτὸ γὰρ ἑωυτῷ συνεχές ἐστι τὸ στῆθος καὶ τῇ ῥάχει.

Τὸ μὲν οὖν ἑαυτῷ συνεχὲς εἶναι τὸ στέρνον ἐναργῶς φαίνεται· τὸ δὲ τῇ ῥάχει νοηθήσεται σαφῶς, ἐὰν σκελετῷ ζώῳ τὰς πλευράς ποτε ἴδῃς ἐναργῶς ἐρηρεισμένας ὀπίσω μὲν ἐπὶ τῆς ῥάχεως, ἔμπροσθεν δὲ πρὸς τὸ στέρνον.
Ἄγχιστα μὲν ἡ κληῒς πρὸς τὸ τοῦ ὤμου ἄρθρον πλοώδης ἐστίν· ἠνάγκασται γὰρ πυκινοκίνητος εἶναι διὰ τὴν τῆς ἀκρωμίης σύζευξιν.
ἄλλως τε ὅταν τρωθῇ, φεύγει ἐς τὸ ἄνω μέρος τὸ πρὸς τῷ στήθει προσεχόμενον καὶ οὐ μάλα ἐς τὸ κάτω μέρος ἀναγκάζεσθαι ἐθέλει.
καὶ γὰρ πέφυκε κοῦφον καὶ ἡ εὐρυχωρίη αὐτῷ ἄνω πλείων ἢ κάτω.
ὁ δὲ ὦμος καὶ τὰ προσηρτημένα τούτοισιν εὐαπόλυτά εἰσιν ἀπὸ τῶν πλευρέων καὶ τοῦ στήθεος καὶ διὰ τοῦτο δύναται καὶ ἀνωτέρω πουλὺ ἀνάγεσθαι καὶ κατωτέρω.
english_sentences: [413] For the chest is continuous both with itself and with the spine.

That the breastbone is continuous with itself is plainly evident; that it is continuous with the spine will be clearly understood if you ever see, in a skeleton of an animal, the ribs plainly resting behind upon the spine and in front against the breastbone.
Nearest to the joint of the shoulder the collarbone is loose (?); for it is compelled to be frequently moved on account of its junction with the acromion.
Besides, when it is injured, the part attached at the chest escapes upward, and is not very willing to be forced into the lower position.
For it is naturally light, and the open space for it is greater above than below.
But the shoulder and the parts attached to these are easily detached from the ribs and the chest, and for this reason it can be drawn both much higher and lower.

beads.greek: ὅταν [414] γοῦν καταγῇ κληῒς, τὸ πρὸς τῷ ὤμῳ ὀστέον ἐς τὸ κατωτέρω ἐπιῤῥέπει· ἐς τοῦτο γὰρ ἐπιτροχώτερον αὐτὸ ἅμα τῷ ὤμῳ καὶ τῷ βραχίονι κάτω ῥεῦσαι μᾶλλον ἢ ἐς τὸ ἄνω.
beads.english: When, [414] at any rate, the collarbone is broken, the bone toward the shoulder inclines downward; for it is more readily disposed to slide downward together with the shoulder and the upper arm than upward.

beads.greek: ὁπότε οὖν ταῦτά ἐστιν, ἀξυνετέουσιν ὅσοι τὸ ὑπερέχον τοῦ ὀστέου ἐς τὸ κάτω καταναγκάσαι οἴονται εἶναι, ἀλλὰ δῆλον ὅτι τὸ κάτω πρὸς τῷ ἄνω προσακτέον ἐστί.
beads.english: Since, then, these things are so, those who think that the projecting part of the bone is to be forced downward are without understanding; rather, it is clear that the lower part must be brought up to the upper.

beads.greek: τοῦτο γὰρ ἔχει κίνησιν, τοῦτο γάρ ἐστι καὶ τὸ ἀποστὰν ἀπὸ τῆς φύσιος.
beads.english: For this is the part that has movement; this is also the part that has departed from its natural position.

beads.greek: δῆλον οὖν ὅτι ἄλλως μὲν οὐδαμῶς ἐστιν ἀναγκάσαι τοῦτο· αἵ τε γὰρ ἐπιδέσιες οὐδέν τι μᾶλλον προσαναγκάζουσιν ἢ ἀπαναγκάζουσιν.
beads.english: It is clear, then, that there is no other way at all of forcing this into place; for bandagings do not press it toward the other part any more than they press it away.

beads.greek: εἰ δέ τις τὸν βραχίονα πρὸς τῇσι πλευρῇσιν ὡς μάλιστα ἐόντα ἀναγκάζοι ἄνω, ὡς ὅτι ὀξύτατος ὁ ὦμος φαίνεται εἶναι, δῆλον ὅτι οὕτως ἂν ἁρμοσθείη πρὸς τὸ ὀστέον τὸ ἀπὸ τοῦ στήθεος πεφυκὸς ὅθεν ἀπεσπάσθη.
beads.english: But if one were to force the upper arm upward while it is as close as possible to the ribs, so that the shoulder appears as sharp as possible, it is clear that in this way it would be fitted to the bone that grows from the chest, from which it was torn away.

greek_sentences: ὅταν [414] γοῦν καταγῇ κληῒς, τὸ πρὸς τῷ ὤμῳ ὀστέον ἐς τὸ κατωτέρω ἐπιῤῥέπει· ἐς τοῦτο γὰρ ἐπιτροχώτερον αὐτὸ ἅμα τῷ ὤμῳ καὶ τῷ βραχίονι κάτω ῥεῦσαι μᾶλλον ἢ ἐς τὸ ἄνω.

δῆλον οὖν ὅτι ἄλλως μὲν οὐδαμῶς ἐστιν ἀναγκάσαι τοῦτο· αἵ τε γὰρ ἐπιδέσιες οὐδέν τι μᾶλλον προσαναγκάζουσιν ἢ ἀπαναγκάζουσιν.

εἰ δέ τις τὸν βραχίονα πρὸς τῇσι πλευρῇσιν ὡς μάλιστα ἐόντα ἀναγκάζοι ἄνω, ὡς ὅτι ὀξύτατος ὁ ὦμος φαίνεται εἶναι, δῆλον ὅτι οὕτως ἂν ἁρμοσθείη πρὸς τὸ ὀστέον τὸ ἀπὸ τοῦ στήθεος πεφυκὸς ὅθεν ἀπεσπάσθη.
english_sentences: When, [414] at any rate, the collarbone is broken, the bone toward the shoulder inclines downward; for it is more readily disposed to slide downward together with the shoulder and the upper arm than upward.

Since, then, these things are so, those who think that the projecting part of the bone is to be forced downward are without understanding; rather, it is clear that the lower part must be brought up to the upper.
For this is the part that has movement; this is also the part that has departed from its natural position.
It is clear, then, that there is no other way at all of forcing this into place; for bandagings do not press it toward the other part any more than they press it away.

But if one were to force the upper arm upward while it is as close as possible to the ribs, so that the shoulder appears as sharp as possible, it is clear that in this way it would be fitted to the bone that grows from the chest, from which it was torn away.

beads.greek: Τροπικοῖς ὀνόμασι καὶ γλωσσηματικοῖς εἴωθεν ὁ Ἱπποκράτης ἐννοιῶν χρῆσθαι, καίτοι πολιτικὴν ἑρμηνεύων ἑρμηνείαν, ὅμοιόν τι τούτῳ πεπονθὼς ὁ Ξενοφῶν· καὶ [415] γὰρ ἐκεῖνος εἴπερ τις καὶ ἄλλος ἑρμηνεύων πολιτικῶς, ὅμως παρεμβάλλει πολλάκις ὀνόματα γλωσσηματικὰ καὶ τροπικά.
beads.english: Hippocrates is accustomed to use figurative and glossematic words for his ideas, even though he writes in a civic style of expression. Xenophon is in a similar case: [415] he too, if anyone does, expresses himself in the civic manner, yet he often inserts glossematic and figurative words.

beads.greek: σπανιώτερον μὲν οὖν παρ’ ἐκείνῳ τὸ τοιοῦτον, συνεχέστερον δὲ παρὰ τῷ Ἱπποκράτει, καθάπερ ἐπὶ τῇ προγεγραμμένῃ ῥήσει τὸν κιγκλισμὸν εἶπεν, ἐνταῦθά τε τὸ πλοώδης ἐστίν.
beads.english: This is rarer with Xenophon and more frequent with Hippocrates. So in the passage written earlier he used the word 'kinklismos' (wagtail-like flicking), and here there is 'plōōdēs' ('floating').

beads.greek: ἐνδείκνυται γὰρ διὰ τῆς φωνῆς τὸ οἷον ἀστήρικτος, ᾧ καὶ τὸ ζῶον φαινόμενον μαρτυρεῖ, καθ’ ὅ φησιν ἠνάγκαστο, καθ’ ὃ πυκινοκίνητος αὐτὸς ἐδήλωσεν εἰπὼν, διὰ τὴν τῆς ἀκρωμίης σύζευξιν.
beads.english: By this word he indicates something like 'unsupported'. The appearance of the animal [ζῶον φαινόμενον, text doubtful] also bears witness to this.

beads.greek: αὕτη δὲ πάλιν ἡ ἀκρωμίη διὰ τὸ κατ’ ὦμον ἄρθρον ἐστὶ πυκινοκίνητος, ἀτενὴς, ἅτε ὑπάρχων αὐτὸς καὶ μεγίστας ἔχων κινήσεις.
beads.english: With regard to this he says 'it had been forced', and with regard to this he himself made the point clear by saying 'frequently moved' [πυκινοκίνητος], on account of its junction with the acromion.

beads.greek: τὸ δὲ κατ’ ἀρχὴν εἰρημένον τῆς ῥήσεως, τὸ ἄγχιστα μὲν τὴν ἀμφιβολίαν ἣν ἔχει πρότερον ἐπὶ τοῦ χωρίου προσῆκεν ἀκούειν ἢ τοῦ πράγματος αὐτοῦ.
beads.english: This acromion in turn is frequently moved, and taut [ἀτενής, sense doubtful], on account of the shoulder joint, since the joint itself [ἅτε ὑπάρχων αὐτός, construction doubtful] also has the greatest movements. As for what is said at the beginning of the passage, 'ἄγχιστα μέν' ('nearest'), given the ambiguity it carries, it ought rather to be understood of the place than of the thing itself.

greek_sentences: Τροπικοῖς ὀνόμασι καὶ γλωσσηματικοῖς εἴωθεν ὁ Ἱπποκράτης ἐννοιῶν χρῆσθαι, καίτοι πολιτικὴν ἑρμηνεύων ἑρμηνείαν, ὅμοιόν τι τούτῳ πεπονθὼς ὁ Ξενοφῶν· καὶ [415] γὰρ ἐκεῖνος εἴπερ τις καὶ ἄλλος ἑρμηνεύων πολιτικῶς, ὅμως παρεμβάλλει πολλάκις ὀνόματα γλωσσηματικὰ καὶ τροπικά.
σπανιώτερον μὲν οὖν παρ’ ἐκείνῳ τὸ τοιοῦτον, συνεχέστερον δὲ παρὰ τῷ Ἱπποκράτει, καθάπερ ἐπὶ τῇ προγεγραμμένῃ ῥήσει τὸν κιγκλισμὸν εἶπεν, ἐνταῦθά τε τὸ πλοώδης ἐστίν.
ἐνδείκνυται γὰρ διὰ τῆς φωνῆς τὸ οἷον ἀστήρικτος, ᾧ καὶ τὸ ζῶον φαινόμενον μαρτυρεῖ, καθ’ ὅ φησιν ἠνάγκαστο, καθ’ ὃ πυκινοκίνητος αὐτὸς ἐδήλωσεν εἰπὼν, διὰ τὴν τῆς ἀκρωμίης σύζευξιν.

english_sentences: Hippocrates is accustomed to use figurative and glossematic words for his ideas, even though he writes in a civic style of expression.
Xenophon is in a similar case: [415] he too, if anyone does, expresses himself in the civic manner, yet he often inserts glossematic and figurative words.
This is rarer with Xenophon and more frequent with Hippocrates.
So in the passage written earlier he used the word 'kinklismos' (wagtail-like flicking), and here there is 'plōōdēs' ('floating').
By this word he indicates something like 'unsupported'.
The appearance of the animal [ζῶον φαινόμενον, text doubtful] also bears witness to this.
With regard to this he says 'it had been forced', and with regard to this he himself made the point clear by saying 'frequently moved' [πυκινοκίνητος], on account of its junction with the acromion.

This acromion in turn is frequently moved, and taut [ἀτενής, sense doubtful], on account of the shoulder joint, since the joint itself [ἅτε ὑπάρχων αὐτός, construction doubtful] also has the greatest movements.
As for what is said at the beginning of the passage, 'ἄγχιστα μέν' ('nearest'), given the ambiguity it carries, it ought rather to be understood of the place than of the thing itself.

beads.greek: δῆλον μὲν γὰρ ἐγγυτάτω, ἀλλ’ ἤτοι πλησίον τοῦ ἄρθρου πυκινοκίνητον ἐνδείξεται τὴν κλεῖν εἰρημένον, ὅπερ ἐμοὶ δοκεῖ μᾶλλον ἄν τις ἀκούῃ ὀρθῶς, ἐνίοις ἔδοξε συνάπτειν τὸ ἄγχιστα, δεήσει τὸ πυκινοκίνητον εἶναι [416] τὸ λεγόμενον, τὸ οὕτω ἐγγυτάτω τὸ πυκινοκινήτου ἡ κλείς ἐστι πλησίον τοῦ κατ’ ὦμον ἄρθρου.
beads.english: For it is clear that it means 'nearest'; but either, if said with reference to the place, it will indicate that the collarbone is very mobile (πυκινοκίνητον) near the joint, which seems to me the more correct way to take it, if one understands it rightly; or, as some have thought, if one is to join 'nearest' (ἄγχιστα) with what follows, then 'very mobile' will have to be [416] what is meant, namely: in this way 'nearest' to the very mobile [joint] is the collarbone, near the shoulder joint.

beads.greek: Εἰ οὖν τις τῇ μὲν ἐπιδέσει χρῷτο τῇ νομίμῃ τοῦ ταχέως συναλθεσθῆναι εἵνεκα, ἡγήσαιτο δὲ τἄλλα πάντα μάτην εἶναι παρὰ τὸ σχῆμα τὸ εἰρημένον, ὀρθῶς τε ἂν ξυνίῃ, ἰητρεύοι τ’ ἂν τάχιστα καὶ κάλλιστα· κατακέεσθαι μέντοι τὸν ἄνθρωπον μέγα τὸ διάφορόν ἐστι καὶ ἡμέραι ἱκαναὶ τεσσαρεσκαίδεκα, εἰ ἀτρεμέοι, εἴκοσι δὲ πάμπολλαι. Νομίμην ἐπίδεσιν λέγει τὴν ὑπὸ πάντων εἰθισμένην καὶ ὥσπερ ἄγραφον ἤδη νόμον οὖσαν· οὕτως γὰρ κἀν τῷ βίῳ τινὰ τῶν ἐθῶν, ὅσα πρὸς ἁπάντων ἐπιτηδεύηται, τοῖς νόμοις ἐστὶ παραπλήσια.
beads.english: 'If, then, someone were to use the customary bandaging for the sake of a quick knitting together, but were to consider everything else, apart from the posture that has been described, to be useless, he would both understand rightly and treat most quickly and most finely; it makes a great difference, however, that the patient lie down; and fourteen days are sufficient, if he keeps still, and twenty are more than enough.' By 'customary bandaging' he means that which is habitually used by everyone and has by now become, as it were, an unwritten law; for so too in life certain customs, those practised by all, are closely akin to laws.

beads.greek: τὴν μὲν οὖν καταγματικὴν ἐπίδεσιν οὐ πάντῃ ἐποίουν τοῦ προσήκοντος, καὶ διὰ τοῦτο πλείονα περὶ αὐτῆς ἔγραψεν ἐν πρώτῳ βιβλίῳ περὶ τῶν ἀγμῶν.
beads.english: Now the bandaging for fractures they did not perform altogether as it ought to be done, and for this reason he wrote more about it in the first book On Fractures.

'If, then, someone were to use the customary bandaging for the sake of a quick knitting together, but were to consider everything else, apart from the posture that has been described, to be useless, he would both understand rightly and treat most quickly and most finely; it makes a great difference, however, that the patient lie down; and fourteen days are sufficient, if he keeps still, and twenty are more than enough.' beads.greek: ἐνταυθοῖ δὲ οὐδεμία παθήματος ἐπίδεσις οὐδενὸς [417] τοιαύτη.
beads.english: Here, however, the bandaging of no affection is of this kind.

beads.greek: δέδεικται γάρ μοι καὶ διὰ τῶν εἰς ἐκεῖνο τὸ βιβλίον ὑπομνημάτων, ἀλλὰ καὶ νῦν ἀνεμνήσθη, πάντα μὲν ὅσα τῷ τρόπῳ τῆς καταγματικῆς ἐπιδέσεως ὑποπίπτει παθήματα, κατ’ ἐκεῖνο τὸ βιβλίον ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ γεγράφθαι, πάντα δ’ αὖ πάλιν ὅσα τῇ λοιπῇ κατὰ τοῦτο. γίνεται γὰρ ἡ καταγματικὴ περιβαλλόντων ἡμῶν ἐν κύκλῳ τὰ ὀθόνια τῷ κατεαγότι μορίῳ.
beads.english: [417] For I have shown this both in the commentaries on that book, and it has now been recalled as well: all the affections that fall under the method of fracture bandaging were written by him in that book, and all those, in turn, that fall under the remaining kind in this one.

beads.greek: τὸ δεύτερον εἶδος τῆς ἐπιδέσεως ἐπ’ ἄλλα μόρια τὴν νομὴν ποιουμένων, καὶ κατά γε τὸ πλεῖστον ἐπὶ τὰ ἀντικείμενα τῷ πεπονθότι, καθάπερ κἀν ἰητρείῳ εἶπεν· ὁμολογέει δὲ ὁμοῦ μὲν ἡ περὶ τὴν ἑτέρην μασχάλην περιβολή. Εἰ μέντοι τινὶ ἐπὶ τἀναντία ἡ κληῒς καταγείη, ὃ οὐ μάλιστα γίνεται, ὥστε τὸ μὲν ἀπὸ τοῦ στήθεος ὀστέον ὑποδεδυκέναι, τὸ δὲ ἀπὸ τῆς ἀκρωμίης ὀστέον ὑπερέχειν καὶ ἐποχέεσθαι ἐπὶ τοῦ ἑτέρου, οὐδεμιῆς μεγάλης ἰητρείης ταῦτά γ’ ἂν δέοιτο.
beads.english: For fracture bandaging is done when we wrap the linen strips in a circle around the fractured part; the second kind of bandaging, when we carry the distribution onto other parts, and for the most part onto those opposite to the affected one, as he said also in the Surgery: 'and at the same time the wrapping around the other armpit is consistent with this.' If, however, in someone the collarbone should be fractured the opposite way, which does not very often happen, so that the bone from the chest has sunk beneath while the bone from the acromion projects and rides upon the other, these would require no great treatment.

greek_sentences: ἐνταυθοῖ δὲ οὐδεμία παθήματος ἐπίδεσις οὐδενὸς [417] τοιαύτη.

γίνεται γὰρ ἡ καταγματικὴ περιβαλλόντων ἡμῶν ἐν κύκλῳ τὰ ὀθόνια τῷ κατεαγότι μορίῳ.

τὸ δεύτερον εἶδος τῆς ἐπιδέσεως ἐπ’ ἄλλα μόρια τὴν νομὴν ποιουμένων, καὶ κατά γε τὸ πλεῖστον ἐπὶ τὰ ἀντικείμενα τῷ πεπονθότι, καθάπερ κἀν ἰητρείῳ εἶπεν· ὁμολογέει δὲ ὁμοῦ μὲν ἡ περὶ τὴν ἑτέρην μασχάλην περιβολή.

Εἰ μέντοι τινὶ ἐπὶ τἀναντία ἡ κληῒς καταγείη, ὃ οὐ μάλιστα γίνεται, ὥστε τὸ μὲν ἀπὸ τοῦ στήθεος ὀστέον ὑποδεδυκέναι, τὸ δὲ ἀπὸ τῆς ἀκρωμίης ὀστέον ὑπερέχειν καὶ ἐποχέεσθαι ἐπὶ τοῦ ἑτέρου, οὐδεμιῆς μεγάλης ἰητρείης ταῦτά γ’ ἂν δέοιτο.
english_sentences: Here, however, the bandaging of no affection is of this kind.

[417] For I have shown this both in the commentaries on that book, and it has now been recalled as well: all the affections that fall under the method of fracture bandaging were written by him in that book, and all those, in turn, that fall under the remaining kind in this one.

For fracture bandaging is done when we wrap the linen strips in a circle around the fractured part; the second kind of bandaging, when we carry the distribution onto other parts, and for the most part onto those opposite to the affected one, as he said also in the Surgery: 'and at the same time the wrapping around the other armpit is consistent with this.' If, however, in someone the collarbone should be fractured the opposite way, which does not very often happen, so that the bone from the chest has sunk beneath while the bone from the acromion projects and rides upon the other, these would require no great treatment.

beads.greek: αὐτὸς γὰρ ὁ ὦμος ἀφιέμενος καὶ [418] ὁ βραχίων ἱδρύοι ἂν τὰ ὀστέα πρὸς ἄλληλα καὶ φαύλη ἄν τις ἐπίδεσις ἀρκέοι καὶ ὀλίγαι ἡμέραι τῆς πωρώσιος γένοιτ’ ἄν.
beads.english: For the shoulder itself, when let go, together with [418] the upper arm, would settle the bones against one another; a simple bandaging would suffice, and the formation of callus would take only a few days.

beads.greek: Ἔμπροσθεν μὲν ἔλεγεν, ὡς τὸ πολὺ τὸ ἀπὸ τοῦ στέρνου μέρος τῆς κλειδὸς, ὁπόταν ὅλη δι’ ὅλης ἑαυτῆς ἀποκαυλισθῇ, πρὸς τὴν ἄνω χώραν μεθίσταται, ταπεινότερον δὲ γίγνεσθαι τὸ ἀπὸ τῆς ἀκρωμίης.
beads.english: Earlier he said that, for the most part, when the collarbone is snapped right through its whole thickness, the part of the collarbone that comes from the sternum shifts to the upper region, while the part that comes from the acromion becomes lower.

beads.greek: νυνὶ δὲ περὶ τοῦ σπανιωτέρου τρόπου γράφει, καθ’ ὃν ὑψηλότερον μὲν γίνεται ἀπὸ τῆς ἀκρωμίης, ταπεινότερον τὸ πρὸς τῷ στέρνῳ, ὃ καί φησιν εὐιατότερον ὑπάρχειν.
beads.english: Now, however, he writes about the rarer mode, in which the part from the acromion becomes higher and the part next to the sternum lower; this he also says is easier to treat.

beads.greek: αὐτοῦ καθιεμένου συγκαθίσταται καὶ τὸ τῆς κλειδὸς μέρος, ὅσον συνεχές ἐστι τοῦ ἀκρωμίου.
beads.english: When it (the shoulder) is let down, the part of the collarbone continuous with the acromion also settles down along with it.

beads.greek: καὶ οὕτως ἐξ ἴσου τε γενόμενον θατέρῳ τῆς ἐπιδέσεως καὶ τῆς θεραπείας τυγχάνειν.
beads.english: And thus, having come level with the other part, it receives the bandaging and the treatment.

greek_sentences: αὐτὸς γὰρ ὁ ὦμος ἀφιέμενος καὶ [418] ὁ βραχίων ἱδρύοι ἂν τὰ ὀστέα πρὸς ἄλληλα καὶ φαύλη ἄν τις ἐπίδεσις ἀρκέοι καὶ ὀλίγαι ἡμέραι τῆς πωρώσιος γένοιτ’ ἄν.
Ἔμπροσθεν μὲν ἔλεγεν, ὡς τὸ πολὺ τὸ ἀπὸ τοῦ στέρνου μέρος τῆς κλειδὸς, ὁπόταν ὅλη δι’ ὅλης ἑαυτῆς ἀποκαυλισθῇ, πρὸς τὴν ἄνω χώραν μεθίσταται, ταπεινότερον δὲ γίγνεσθαι τὸ ἀπὸ τῆς ἀκρωμίης.
νυνὶ δὲ περὶ τοῦ σπανιωτέρου τρόπου γράφει, καθ’ ὃν ὑψηλότερον μὲν γίνεται ἀπὸ τῆς ἀκρωμίης, ταπεινότερον τὸ πρὸς τῷ στέρνῳ, ὃ καί φησιν εὐιατότερον ὑπάρχειν.
αὐτοῦ καθιεμένου συγκαθίσταται καὶ τὸ τῆς κλειδὸς μέρος, ὅσον συνεχές ἐστι τοῦ ἀκρωμίου.
καὶ οὕτως ἐξ ἴσου τε γενόμενον θατέρῳ τῆς ἐπιδέσεως καὶ τῆς θεραπείας τυγχάνειν.
english_sentences: For the shoulder itself, when let go, together with [418] the upper arm, would settle the bones against one another; a simple bandaging would suffice, and the formation of callus would take only a few days.

Earlier he said that, for the most part, when the collarbone is snapped right through its whole thickness, the part of the collarbone that comes from the sternum shifts to the upper region, while the part that comes from the acromion becomes lower.
Now, however, he writes about the rarer mode, in which the part from the acromion becomes higher and the part next to the sternum lower; this he also says is easier to treat.
When it (the shoulder) is let down, the part of the collarbone continuous with the acromion also settles down along with it.
And thus, having come level with the other part, it receives the bandaging and the treatment.

beads.greek: Εἰ δὲ μὴ καταγείη μὲν οὕτως, παρολισθαίνοι δὲ ἐς τὸ πλάγιον ἢ τῇ ἢ τῇ, ἐς τὴν φύσιν μὲν ἀπαγαγεῖν ἂν δέοι, [419] ἀναγαγόντα τὸν ὦμον σὺν τῷ βραχίονι, ὥσπερ καὶ πρόσθεν εἴρηται.
beads.english: But if it is not broken in this way, but slips aside laterally, to one side or the other, one would need to bring it back into its natural position, [419] raising the shoulder together with the upper arm, just as has also been said before.

beads.greek: ὅταν δὲ ἵζηται εἰς τὴν ἀρχαίην φύσιν, ταχείη ἂν ἡ ἄλλη ἰητρείη εἴη.
beads.english: And when it settles into its original natural position, the rest of the treatment would be quick.

beads.greek: τὰ μὲν οὖν πλεῖστα τῶν παρηλλαγμένων κατορθοῖ αὐτὸς ὁ βραχίων ἀναγκαζόμενος πρὸς τὰ ἄνω.
beads.english: Most of the parts that have been displaced are, then, set right by the upper arm itself when it is forced upwards.

beads.greek: Ἀκούειν σε χρὴ νῦν εἰρῆσθαι πρὸς αὐτοῦ κατὰ τὴν ἔνδον ἢ ἔξω μετάστασιν τῶν ὀστῶν.
beads.english: You must understand that this has now been said by him with reference to the displacement of the bones inward or outward.

beads.greek: ἄκουε δέ μου λέγοντος ἔνδον μὲν εἰς τὸ βάθος τοῦ σώματος, ἔξω δὲ ἐπὶ τοῦ πρὸς τὸ δέρμα.
beads.english: And understand me, when I say 'inward', to mean into the depth of the body, and 'outward' to mean towards the skin.

greek_sentences: Εἰ δὲ μὴ καταγείη μὲν οὕτως, παρολισθαίνοι δὲ ἐς τὸ πλάγιον ἢ τῇ ἢ τῇ, ἐς τὴν φύσιν μὲν ἀπαγαγεῖν ἂν δέοι, [419] ἀναγαγόντα τὸν ὦμον σὺν τῷ βραχίονι, ὥσπερ καὶ πρόσθεν εἴρηται.
ὅταν δὲ ἵζηται εἰς τὴν ἀρχαίην φύσιν, ταχείη ἂν ἡ ἄλλη ἰητρείη εἴη.
τὰ μὲν οὖν πλεῖστα τῶν παρηλλαγμένων κατορθοῖ αὐτὸς ὁ βραχίων ἀναγκαζόμενος πρὸς τὰ ἄνω.
Ἀκούειν σε χρὴ νῦν εἰρῆσθαι πρὸς αὐτοῦ κατὰ τὴν ἔνδον ἢ ἔξω μετάστασιν τῶν ὀστῶν.
ἄκουε δέ μου λέγοντος ἔνδον μὲν εἰς τὸ βάθος τοῦ σώματος, ἔξω δὲ ἐπὶ τοῦ πρὸς τὸ δέρμα.
english_sentences: But if it is not broken in this way, but slips aside laterally, to one side or the other, one would need to bring it back into its natural position, [419] raising the shoulder together with the upper arm, just as has also been said before.
And when it settles into its original natural position, the rest of the treatment would be quick.
Most of the parts that have been displaced are, then, set right by the upper arm itself when it is forced upwards.
You must understand that this has now been said by him with reference to the displacement of the bones inward or outward.
And understand me, when I say 'inward', to mean into the depth of the body, and 'outward' to mean towards the skin.

beads.greek: Ὅσα δὲ τῶν ἄνωθεν παρολισθαίνοντα ἐς τὸ πλάγιον ἦλθεν ἢ ἐς τὸ κατωτέρω, συμπορσύνοι ἂν τὴν κατόρθωσιν, εἰ ὁ μὲν ἄνθρωπος ὕπτιος κέοιτο, κατὰ δὲ τὸ μεσηγὺ τῶν ὠμοπλατέων ὑψηλότερόν τι ὀλίγον ὑποκέοιτο, ὡς περιῤῥηδὲς ἔῃ τὸ στῆθος ὡς μάλιστα καὶ τὸν βραχίονα, εἰ ἀνάγοι [420] τις παρὰ τὰς πλευρὰς παρατεταμένον.
beads.english: In those cases where the upper [fragments], slipping, have passed to the side or lower down, it would contribute to the correction if the person were to lie supine, and something a little higher were placed beneath him in the region between the shoulder blades, so that the chest is as far as possible bent over [περιρρηδές]; and [it would contribute] if someone were to draw the upper arm upward, stretched out alongside the ribs.

beads.greek: ὁ δὲ ἰητρὸς τῇ μὲν ἑτέρῃ χειρὶ ἐς τὴν κεφαλὴν τοῦ βραχίονος ἐμβαλὼν τὸ θέναρ τῆς χειρὸς ἀπωθέοι, τῇ δ’ ἑτέρῃ τὰ ὀστέα τὰ κατεαγότα εὐθετίζοι, οὕτως ἂν μάλιστα ἐς τὴν φύσιν ἄγοι.
beads.english: And if the physician, with one hand, placing the flat of the hand on the head of the upper arm, were to push it away, and with the other were to set the broken bones in line, in this way he would best bring them into their natural position.

beads.greek: ἀτὰρ ὅπερ ἤδη εἴρηται, εὖ μάλα τὸ ἄνωθεν ὀστέον ἐς τὸ κάτω φιλέει ὑποδύνειν.
beads.english: But, as has already been said, the upper bone is very much inclined to slip in under, downward.

beads.greek: τοῖσι μὲν οὖν πλείστοισιν ὅταν ἐπιδεθῶσι, τὸ σχῆμα ἀρήγει, παρ’ αὐτὰς τὰς πλευρὰς τὸν ἀγκῶνα ἔχοντα οὕτως ἐς τὸ ἄνω τὸν ὦμον ἀναγκάζεσθαι.
beads.english: In most cases, then, once they have been bandaged, the posture helps: with the elbow held right against the ribs, the shoulder is in this way forced upward.

beads.greek: ἔστι δ’ οἷσι μὲν τὸν ὦμον ἀναγκάζειν δεῖ ἐς τὸ ἄνω, ὡς εἴρηται.
beads.english: And there are some in whom one must force the shoulder upward, as has been said.

beads.greek: Ὅταν οὖν τὸ συνεχὲς τῶν στέρνων μέρος τῆς κλειδὸς ἢ εἰς τὸ πλάγιον ἢ εἰς τὸ κάτω παρολισθῇ, τηνικαῦτά φησι συμπαρασκευάζεσθαι εἰς τὴν κατόρθωσιν, εἴ τις τὸν ἄνθρωπον ὕπτιον κατακλίνας ὑποθείη μεταξὺ τῶν ὠμοπλατῶν κατ’ αὐτὴν τὴν ῥάχιν, δηλονότι προσκεφάλαιον ἢ ὑπαυχένιον ἤ τι τοιοῦτον, ὡς περικεκλασμένον κατὰ τοῦτο γίνεσθαι τὸν θώρακα σύμπαντα.
beads.english: So when the part of the collarbone that is continuous with the sternum slips either to the side or downward, he says that it then helps to prepare for the correction if, having laid the person down supine, one places beneath him between the shoulder blades, at the spine itself, a pillow, obviously, or a neck-cushion or something of the sort, so that the whole thorax becomes bent around at this point.

beads.greek: τὸ γὰρ περιῤῥηδὲς ἔῃ οὕτως εἴρηται καὶ παρὰ τῷ ποιητῇ· Περιῤῥηδής τε τραπέζης κατέπεσε.
beads.english: For 'that it be bent over' (περιρρηδὲς ἔῃ) is said in this sense also in the Poet: 'and doubled over the table he fell.'

greek_sentences: Ὅσα δὲ τῶν ἄνωθεν παρολισθαίνοντα ἐς τὸ πλάγιον ἦλθεν ἢ ἐς τὸ κατωτέρω, συμπορσύνοι ἂν τὴν κατόρθωσιν, εἰ ὁ μὲν ἄνθρωπος ὕπτιος κέοιτο, κατὰ δὲ τὸ μεσηγὺ τῶν ὠμοπλατέων ὑψηλότερόν τι ὀλίγον ὑποκέοιτο, ὡς περιῤῥηδὲς ἔῃ τὸ στῆθος ὡς μάλιστα καὶ τὸν βραχίονα, εἰ ἀνάγοι [420] τις παρὰ τὰς πλευρὰς παρατεταμένον.
ὁ δὲ ἰητρὸς τῇ μὲν ἑτέρῃ χειρὶ ἐς τὴν κεφαλὴν τοῦ βραχίονος ἐμβαλὼν τὸ θέναρ τῆς χειρὸς ἀπωθέοι, τῇ δ’ ἑτέρῃ τὰ ὀστέα τὰ κατεαγότα εὐθετίζοι, οὕτως ἂν μάλιστα ἐς τὴν φύσιν ἄγοι.
ἀτὰρ ὅπερ ἤδη εἴρηται, εὖ μάλα τὸ ἄνωθεν ὀστέον ἐς τὸ κάτω φιλέει ὑποδύνειν.
τοῖσι μὲν οὖν πλείστοισιν ὅταν ἐπιδεθῶσι, τὸ σχῆμα ἀρήγει, παρ’ αὐτὰς τὰς πλευρὰς τὸν ἀγκῶνα ἔχοντα οὕτως ἐς τὸ ἄνω τὸν ὦμον ἀναγκάζεσθαι.
ἔστι δ’ οἷσι μὲν τὸν ὦμον ἀναγκάζειν δεῖ ἐς τὸ ἄνω, ὡς εἴρηται.

Ὅταν οὖν τὸ συνεχὲς τῶν στέρνων μέρος τῆς κλειδὸς ἢ εἰς τὸ πλάγιον ἢ εἰς τὸ κάτω παρολισθῇ, τηνικαῦτά φησι συμπαρασκευάζεσθαι εἰς τὴν κατόρθωσιν, εἴ τις τὸν ἄνθρωπον ὕπτιον κατακλίνας ὑποθείη μεταξὺ τῶν ὠμοπλατῶν κατ’ αὐτὴν τὴν ῥάχιν, δηλονότι προσκεφάλαιον ἢ ὑπαυχένιον ἤ τι τοιοῦτον, ὡς περικεκλασμένον κατὰ τοῦτο γίνεσθαι τὸν θώρακα σύμπαντα.
τὸ γὰρ περιῤῥηδὲς ἔῃ οὕτως εἴρηται καὶ παρὰ τῷ ποιητῇ· Περιῤῥηδής τε τραπέζης κατέπεσε.
english_sentences: In those cases where the upper [fragments], slipping, have passed to the side or lower down, it would contribute to the correction if the person were to lie supine, and something a little higher were placed beneath him in the region between the shoulder blades, so that the chest is as far as possible bent over [περιρρηδές]; and [it would contribute] if someone were to draw the upper arm upward, stretched out alongside the ribs.

And if the physician, with one hand, placing the flat of the hand on the head of the upper arm, were to push it away, and with the other were to set the broken bones in line, in this way he would best bring them into their natural position.
But, as has already been said, the upper bone is very much inclined to slip in under, downward.
In most cases, then, once they have been bandaged, the posture helps: with the elbow held right against the ribs, the shoulder is in this way forced upward.
And there are some in whom one must force the shoulder upward, as has been said.

So when the part of the collarbone that is continuous with the sternum slips either to the side or downward, he says that it then helps to prepare for the correction if, having laid the person down supine, one places beneath him between the shoulder blades, at the spine itself, a pillow, obviously, or a neck-cushion or something of the sort, so that the whole thorax becomes bent around at this point.
For 'that it be bent over' (περιρρηδὲς ἔῃ) is said in this sense also in the Poet: 'and doubled over the table he fell.'

beads.greek: [421] κατὰ τοῦτον οὖν τὸν τρόπον σχηματισθέντος τοῦ ἀνθρώπου τὸν ἰατρὸν ἀξιοῖ τῇ μὲν ἑτέρᾳ χειρὶ τὴν κεφαλὴν τοῦ βραχίονος διανάγειν παρὰ τὰς πλευρὰς παρατεταμένον ἀπωθεῖν ἐκτός.
beads.english: [421] When the patient has been positioned in this way, he requires the physician, with one hand, to push the head of the upper arm outward, the arm being drawn up (?) extended alongside the ribs.

beads.greek: οὕτως γὰρ ἂν διασταίη μάλιστα τὰ κατεαγότα μόρια τῆς κλειδὸς εἰς τοῦτο καὶ τοῦ περιῤῥηδοῦς σχήματος συντελοῦντος οὐ μικρόν.
beads.english: For in this way the broken parts of the collarbone would be separated as far as possible, the bent-back posture also contributing not a little to this.

beads.greek: διαπλάττειν δὲ τῇ ἑτέρᾳ χειρὶ καὶ συναπάγειν πρὸς ἄλληλα τὰ διεστῶτα τῆς χειρὸς μόρια τὸν βραχίονα πρὸς τὰς πλευρὰς παρατεταμένον ἀνάγοντα κατὰ τὴν ἑξῆς ῥῆσιν ἐνίοτέ φησιν ἄμεινον εἶναι.
beads.english: With the other hand he is to mould them into shape and bring together the parts of the hand (sic; ?collarbone) that have separated, while drawing up the upper arm extended alongside the ribs.

beads.greek: Τὸν δὲ ἀγκῶνα πρὸς τὸ στῆθος παράγειν, ἄκρην δὲ τὴν χεῖρα παρὰ τὸ ἀκρώμιον τοῦ ὑγιέος ὤμου ἴσχειν· ἢν μὲν οὖν κατακέεσθαι τολμᾷ, ἀντιστήριγμά τι προστιθέναι χρὴ, ὡς ἂν ὁ ὦμος ἀνωτάτω ἔῃ, ἢν δὲ περιίῃ, σφενδόνην χρὴ ἐκ ταινίης περὶ τὸ ὀξὺ τοῦ ἀγκῶνος ποιήσαντα ἀναλαμβάνειν περὶ τὸν αὐχένα.
beads.english: In the next passage he says that it is sometimes better: "To bring the elbow forward to the chest, and to hold the extremity of the hand against the acromion of the healthy shoulder. If, then, the patient can bring himself to lie down, one must put some counter-support in place, so that the shoulder may be as high as possible; but if he walks about, one must make a sling out of a band around the point of the elbow and suspend it around the neck."

greek_sentences: [421] κατὰ τοῦτον οὖν τὸν τρόπον σχηματισθέντος τοῦ ἀνθρώπου τὸν ἰατρὸν ἀξιοῖ τῇ μὲν ἑτέρᾳ χειρὶ τὴν κεφαλὴν τοῦ βραχίονος διανάγειν παρὰ τὰς πλευρὰς παρατεταμένον ἀπωθεῖν ἐκτός.
οὕτως γὰρ ἂν διασταίη μάλιστα τὰ κατεαγότα μόρια τῆς κλειδὸς εἰς τοῦτο καὶ τοῦ περιῤῥηδοῦς σχήματος συντελοῦντος οὐ μικρόν.
διαπλάττειν δὲ τῇ ἑτέρᾳ χειρὶ καὶ συναπάγειν πρὸς ἄλληλα τὰ διεστῶτα τῆς χειρὸς μόρια τὸν βραχίονα πρὸς τὰς πλευρὰς παρατεταμένον ἀνάγοντα κατὰ τὴν ἑξῆς ῥῆσιν ἐνίοτέ φησιν ἄμεινον εἶναι.

Τὸν δὲ ἀγκῶνα πρὸς τὸ στῆθος παράγειν, ἄκρην δὲ τὴν χεῖρα παρὰ τὸ ἀκρώμιον τοῦ ὑγιέος ὤμου ἴσχειν· ἢν μὲν οὖν κατακέεσθαι τολμᾷ, ἀντιστήριγμά τι προστιθέναι χρὴ, ὡς ἂν ὁ ὦμος ἀνωτάτω ἔῃ, ἢν δὲ περιίῃ, σφενδόνην χρὴ ἐκ ταινίης περὶ τὸ ὀξὺ τοῦ ἀγκῶνος ποιήσαντα ἀναλαμβάνειν περὶ τὸν αὐχένα.
english_sentences: [421] When the patient has been positioned in this way, he requires the physician, with one hand, to push the head of the upper arm outward, the arm being drawn up (?) extended alongside the ribs.
For in this way the broken parts of the collarbone would be separated as far as possible, the bent-back posture also contributing not a little to this.
With the other hand he is to mould them into shape and bring together the parts of the hand (sic; ?collarbone) that have separated, while drawing up the upper arm extended alongside the ribs.
In the next passage he says that it is sometimes better: "To bring the elbow forward to the chest, and to hold the extremity of the hand against the acromion of the healthy shoulder.

If, then, the patient can bring himself to lie down, one must put some counter-support in place, so that the shoulder may be as high as possible; but if he walks about, one must make a sling out of a band around the point of the elbow and suspend it around the neck."

beads.greek: [422] Τὸ δὲ τοιοῦτον σχῆμα πρὸς τὴν ἐκτὸς χώραν ἀπάγει δηλονότι τὴν κεφαλὴν τοῦ βραχίονος, ὡς συναπάγεται καὶ τὸ τῆς κλειδὸς μέρος τὸ συνημμένον τῷ ἀκρωμίῳ, ἀλλ’ οὐκ εἶναι χρείαν φησὶ τοιούτου σχήματος ὡς τὸ πολύ.
beads.english: [422] Such a posture evidently draws the head of the upper arm away to the outer region, so that the part of the collarbone joined to the acromion is drawn away along with it.

beads.greek: γίγνεσθαι γὰρ αὐτάρκως τὴν ἐπανόρθωσιν καὶ διὰ τοῦ προτέρου, καθ’ ὃ περὶ τὰς πλευρὰς ὁ βραχίων παρατεταμένος ἐπήγετο, τοῦ ἀγκῶνος αὐτόθι μένοντος, οὐχ ὥσπερ νῦν ἐπὶ τὸ στῆθος παραγενομένου.
beads.english: But he says that for the most part there is no need of such a posture, for the correction is accomplished sufficiently by the former one as well, in which the upper arm, stretched along the ribs, was brought up while the elbow stayed where it was, and was not brought across to the chest as it is now.

beads.greek: τοῦτ’ οὖν παρέχειν ἐπὶ τὸ στῆθος οὐχ ὡς ἀχρήστου τοῦ προτέρου φευκτέον ἡμῖν ἐστιν, ἀλλ’ ὡς καὶ διακινουμένου τὰ πολλὰ τῆς προκειμένης ἐνεργείας κατορθοῦσθαι δυναμένης.
beads.english: So this bringing of the arm to the chest is to be avoided by us, not as though the former posture were useless, but because, with the former also moving the parts, the operation in hand can for the most part be brought to a successful result.

beads.greek: εἰ δ’ ἐν τῷ πράττειν αὐτὴν μὴ ὑπακούοι τὸ ἔργον, οὕτως ἐπὶ τὸ δεύτερον σχῆμα μεταβησόμεθα.
beads.english: But if, when we perform it, the result does not respond, we shall then pass over to the second posture.

greek_sentences: [422] Τὸ δὲ τοιοῦτον σχῆμα πρὸς τὴν ἐκτὸς χώραν ἀπάγει δηλονότι τὴν κεφαλὴν τοῦ βραχίονος, ὡς συναπάγεται καὶ τὸ τῆς κλειδὸς μέρος τὸ συνημμένον τῷ ἀκρωμίῳ, ἀλλ’ οὐκ εἶναι χρείαν φησὶ τοιούτου σχήματος ὡς τὸ πολύ.
γίγνεσθαι γὰρ αὐτάρκως τὴν ἐπανόρθωσιν καὶ διὰ τοῦ προτέρου, καθ’ ὃ περὶ τὰς πλευρὰς ὁ βραχίων παρατεταμένος ἐπήγετο, τοῦ ἀγκῶνος αὐτόθι μένοντος, οὐχ ὥσπερ νῦν ἐπὶ τὸ στῆθος παραγενομένου.
τοῦτ’ οὖν παρέχειν ἐπὶ τὸ στῆθος οὐχ ὡς ἀχρήστου τοῦ προτέρου φευκτέον ἡμῖν ἐστιν, ἀλλ’ ὡς καὶ διακινουμένου τὰ πολλὰ τῆς προκειμένης ἐνεργείας κατορθοῦσθαι δυναμένης.
εἰ δ’ ἐν τῷ πράττειν αὐτὴν μὴ ὑπακούοι τὸ ἔργον, οὕτως ἐπὶ τὸ δεύτερον σχῆμα μεταβησόμεθα.
english_sentences: [422] Such a posture evidently draws the head of the upper arm away to the outer region, so that the part of the collarbone joined to the acromion is drawn away along with it.

But he says that for the most part there is no need of such a posture, for the correction is accomplished sufficiently by the former one as well, in which the upper arm, stretched along the ribs, was brought up while the elbow stayed where it was, and was not brought across to the chest as it is now.

So this bringing of the arm to the chest is to be avoided by us, not as though the former posture were useless, but because, with the former also moving the parts, the operation in hand can for the most part be brought to a successful result.
But if, when we perform it, the result does not respond, we shall then pass over to the second posture.
